extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of Euclidean geometry (readers studying Euclid, Book I–II)
extracted.subtask_description: Study and prove the propositions of Euclid's Elements (end of Book I and Book II: theory of rectangles), answer examination questions, and solve the listed exercises. Emphasis on geometric proofs and their algebraic correspondences (squares, rectangles, distributive law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for Examination on Book I
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive list of exam questions covering fundamental definitions, elementary constructions, classification, and properties proved in Book I (e.g., 'What is Geometry?', 'What is geometric magnitude?', 'Name the primary concepts of geometry', 'How many conditions are necessary to fix the position of a point in a plane?', 'How many conditions are required to construct a triangle?', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes expected short answers and facts to know (examples given: geometric magnitude = that which has extension in space; primary concepts = points, lines, surfaces, solids; a point in a plane fixed by two conditions; circle requires three conditions: centre position (2) and radius). Also asks candidates to identify obverses, converses, congruence vs identity, to classify properties of triangles and parallelograms, and to give examples from Book I. Use these questions as the syllabus for required knowledge and standard examination topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises on Book I (student tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of constructive and propositional exercises intended to test understanding of Book I results (e.g., proving concurrency of medians, constructing triangles from various data, loci problems, inscribing figures, bisecting polygons, locus/max/min problems, billiard path problems, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises range from routine constructions (construct triangle given two sides and median) to more advanced loci and extremal problems (maximize difference/sum of distances, locus of points with given sum of perpendiculars). Many exercises are geometric formulations of algebraic facts; students are expected to produce Euclidean constructions and rigorous proofs. Use Book I propositions as tools; some exercises encourage using parallels, medians, bisectors, and similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II preliminary theory (Theory of Rectangles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory exposition that every proposition involves a square or rectangle; connects geometric rectangles/squares with algebraic multiplication and powers (square units, rectangle = product of adjacent sides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains square and rectangle units, shows how areas of rectangles relate to multiplication (AB·AD etc.), and motivates using algebraic multiplication to simplify proofs of Book II propositions. Recommends students become acquainted with both geometric and algebraic proofs to better understand meanings of propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions i–vi: segments and points of division (internal/external), rectangle and square definitions, definition of 'rectangle contained by two separate lines', and the gnomon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must know these definitions to follow and construct the proofs in Book II. Example: a rectangle contained by two separate lines AB and CD is the parallelogram formed by erecting a perpendicular at A equal to CD and drawing parallels; a gnomon is the figure remaining when a parallelogram about a diagonal and its complement are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition I (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two lines (A, BC) be such that one is divided into parts (BD, DE, EC), then the rectangle contained by the two lines (A, BC) is equal to the sum of the rectangles contained by A and each part (i.e., A(a+b+c) = Aa + Ab + Ac).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric demonstration via constructing a rectangle on A and BC, decomposing into rectangles on each segment. Illustrated numerically (example: A=6, BD=5, DE=4, EC=3 gives equality 72 = 30+24+18). Corollaries: rectangle with difference equals difference of rectangles; area of triangle = 1/2 · base · perpendicular. This proposition is the geometric analogue of the distributive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition II (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line AB is divided at C into AC and CB, the square on the whole line AB equals the sum of the rectangles contained by the whole and each segment (AB^2 = AB·AC + AB·CB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved as special case of Prop I when the undivided line equals one of the divided segments; also expressed algebraically AB^2 = AB·AC + AB·CB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition III (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line AB be divided at C, the rectangle AB·CB equals the square on CB together with the rectangle AC·CB (AB·CB = CB^2 + AC·CB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof by describing square on CB and relating parallelograms; algebraic form AB·CB = AC·CB + CB^2. Noted as a particular case of Prop I when the undivided line equals a segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition IV (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line AB be divided at C into AC and CB, the square on the whole AB equals the sum of the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB (AB^2 = AC^2 + 2·AC·CB + CB^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric construction decomposing the square on AB into two squares and two equal rectangles; algebraic interpretation as expansion of (AC + CB)^2. Corollaries: parallelograms about a diagonal of a square are squares; square on a line equals four times square on its half.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition V (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB is divided into two equal parts at C and into two unequal parts at D, then the rectangle AD·DB together with the square on CD equals the square on half the line (i.e., AD·DB + CD^2 = CB^2 where CB is half).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof via squares on segments; algebraic derivation: AD·DB + CD^2 = BC^2. Corollaries include difference of squares identity: difference of squares on two lines equals rectangle of their sum and difference; optimization note: among rectangles with fixed perimeter, the square has greatest area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VI (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line AB be bisected at C and divided externally at D, then the rectangle AD·BD together with the square on half the line equals the square on the segment between the middle point and the external division (AD·BD + CB^2 = CD^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric and algebraic proofs given: AD·BD + CB^2 = CD^2 derived by constructing squares and parallelograms. Exercises suggest reducing Prop VI to V by producing the line oppositely and solving external division construction problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VII (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB be divided at C, the sum of the squares on AB and CB equals twice the rectangle AB·CB together with the square on AC (AB^2 + CB^2 = 2·AB·CB + AC^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof offered and also algebraic rearrangement: AC^2 + 2AB·CB = AB^2 + CB^2. Corollaries: relations between square on sum and difference (arithmetic progression) and identities useful for later propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition VIII (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB be divided at C, the square on the sum of AB and BC equals four times the rectangle AB·BC together with the square on AC ( (AB + BC)^2 = 4·AB·BC + AC^2 ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by constructing an extended line and relating squares; shows geometric relation corresponding to algebraic identities involving sum and multiples. Also derived directly from earlier propositions (IV and VII). Exercises include algebraic-style problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition IX (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB be bisected at C and divided into unequal parts at D, the sum of the squares on the unequal parts AD and DB equals twice the sum of the squares on AC and CD (AD^2 + DB^2 = 2·AC^2 + 2·CD^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric construction uses erected right angles and equalities to reduce to sums of squares; algebraic formulation and corollary: sum of squares on segments minimized when bisected. Exercises apply to extremal and partition problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition X (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB be bisected at C and divided externally at D, the sum of the squares on AD and DB equals twice the square on half the line plus twice the square on the segment between points of section (AD^2 + DB^2 = 2·AC^2 + 2·CD^2) (external-division variant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof analogous to Prop IX but for external division; demonstrates how external partitions produce similar square-sum identities. Exercises follow to reduce to internal case and solve construction problems given sums/differences/rectangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises (Book II)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of exercises following the propositions, asking students to prove related identities and apply propositions to problems (e.g., relate perpendicular from vertex to segments of hypotenuse, properties of right-angled triangles, maximize/minimize products or sums under partition constraints, division problems to equate rectangles to squares, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises encourage applying the geometric identities as algebraic tools; several are framed as construction problems (divide a line so rectangle of parts meets a condition), extrema problems (product maximized when parts equal), and connections to inscription problems (e.g., 17-gon). Use Props I–X and corollaries as standard tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological recommendation: use algebraic multiplication alongside geometric proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The text recommends students learn proofs by algebraic multiplication as well as Euclidean constructions to better understand the meaning of each proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is explicit pedagogical guidance: 'We recommend the student to make himself acquainted with the proofs by this method as well as with those of Euclid. He will thus better understand the meaning of each Proposition.' Treat geometric decompositions as visual analogues of algebraic identities (distributive law, expansion of squares).
